parts.title: Using large AI image models to study the tiny worm C. elegans automatically: from measuring body shape in still pictures to following nerve activity in moving worms
parts.abstract:
Scientists in many fields need to measure the features of the tiny roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, such as its body shape, its behavior and its nerve activity. Getting useful data out of microscope pictures is still one of the biggest time drains in this work. The usual way to find a worm in a picture is to sort every pixel by how bright it is and keep the pixels that fall within a chosen brightness range. This method is easily thrown off by changes in lighting, by random speckle in the image (noise), by worms lying on top of each other, or by light that is brighter in some places than others. When it fails, researchers have to set up their experiments very carefully, buy expensive equipment, or spend a lot of time correcting the results by hand. All of this slows them down and can creep in bias.

Here we introduce TWARDIS (Tools for Worm Automated Recognition & Dynamic Imaging System). It is a set of analysis tools written in the Python programming language, built from separate parts that can be swapped or upgraded. It uses large AI models that have already learned to recognize things in pictures, called foundation vision models. In particular, it uses the Segment Anything Models (SAM and SAM2), which are very good at tracing the outline of objects in an image, together with a smaller AI model that we trained to tell worms from other things. With these, TWARDIS overcomes some of the problems above.

We show that this team of AI tools works well across many different kinds of imaging. For measuring body shape in still pictures, TWARDIS sorted out worms lying on top of each other in noisy images without any help from people. Its measurements matched those made by hand with a correlation of 0.999, where 1 would be a perfect match. For behavior tests in which worms swim or crawl, the system traced the worm's body in fine detail even in low-resolution videos that showed a wide area, where the worm took up only about 0.25% of the picture. It correctly captured complicated body bends without throwing away any video frames.

Finally, we used TWARDIS on calcium imaging, a method that uses a glowing dye to show how active a nerve is, in worms that were partly held in place. It traced the separate parts of the nerve precisely, frame by frame. This reduced the false flattening of the signal that often happens with the older approach of measuring only a fixed small patch of the image. It also let us measure the worm's head position in absolute terms, rather than as a relative value.

Because TWARDIS is built from separate parts and can run on more powerful computers, it is easy to use now and easy to improve later without rebuilding it. By automating some of the slowest steps in analyzing images, TWARDIS removes many of the major bottlenecks and trade-offs in C. elegans research. This lets researchers focus on the biological questions they want to answer instead of the technical problems of processing images.
parts.introduction_first: The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans has long been one of the most important animals used in biological research. It is easy to study its genes, its body processes are shared with many other animals, it lives a short life, and it is see-through. These qualities make it extremely useful for studying aging, development, the nervous system and new drugs. A key part of C. elegans research is measuring the worm's features in numbers. This can mean measuring its body shape accurately, describing complicated behaviors, or following the activity of its nerves. Cameras and microscopes have become much easier to get, but pulling useful, high-quality data out of the pictures they take is still a major time drain.
parts.introduction_rest:
In almost every way of measuring a worm's features from pictures, the very first and one of the most important steps is tracing the outline of the worm, or of the body parts we are interested in, and separating it from the background. Scientists call this step segmentation. In the past, it mostly depended on sorting pixels by brightness and on simple computer methods that look for basic shapes and patterns. These methods are well known for being fragile: they react strongly to the small changes that happen from one experiment to the next. Ordinary problems in taking pictures, such as lighting that is brighter in some places than others, parts of the picture that are out of focus, bits of dust or debris in the background, or worms lying on top of each other, often make brightness-based methods fail. The result is a worm outline that is broken into pieces or simply wrong.

To make up for these failures, researchers often spend a lot of effort getting their imaging conditions just right. They may use expensive equipment that takes very sharp, detailed pictures, give up on measuring many features, or spend a great deal of time correcting the results by hand. When scientists follow something that changes over time, such as a worm's behavior or its nerve activity, poor tracing causes real problems. Frames of video may be thrown away, or the signal may be flattened out artificially. Important information about how things change over time is then lost, and real biological effects may go unnoticed. Tools that are partly automated often need a person to mark the area of interest, to adjust settings, or to correct the results by hand. This makes processing take longer, and different people may make different choices, which brings in bias. On top of this, many existing automated tools need special computer setups or paid licenses (for example, MATLAB, C++ or complicated Docker configurations), so fewer people can use them.

Recent progress in deep learning, a kind of AI in which computer programs learn patterns from many examples, has shown promise for studying C. elegans automatically. These approaches are powerful, but many of them needed large collections of pictures that experts had carefully labeled by hand, and those collections were made for particular imaging conditions and particular tasks. To work well in a different experimental setup, they had to be retrained on new examples, which made them very hard to use. Other tools use deep learning for steps that come after tracing, such as recognizing which worm is which, sorting worms into types, or following the same worm from one frame to the next. Even so, they still rely on the older brightness-based method to make the first rough outline, so their measurements that depend on tracing are still affected. So there is still a need for a way to trace the worm that does not depend on sorting pixels by brightness and does not need retraining for each new situation.

A major breakthrough in computer vision, the field of teaching computers to understand pictures, has been the rise of foundation vision models. Some of these are trained on huge, very varied and high-quality collections of pictures. They can take on new tasks with little or no retraining. In particular, the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and its successor, SAM2, can trace the outline of objects in pictures in a way that works in far more situations than ever before. They have also proved remarkably reliable when pictures vary, without any adjustment. These models have already succeeded in medical imaging, in microscopy and in other areas of biology, which suggests they could transform C. elegans research as well.

In this paper, we introduce TWARDIS (Tools for Worm Automated Recognition & Dynamic Imaging System). It is a set of analysis tools written in the Python programming language, built from separate parts that can be swapped or upgraded. It uses these foundation vision models to overcome some long-standing trade-offs in measuring C. elegans features. TWARDIS offers automated, highly precise ways of analyzing pictures that need very little input from the user, and it copes well with many of the imperfect conditions that are common when taking pictures in a regular laboratory. We show how flexible TWARDIS is across four kinds of imaging, each more complex than the last. First, it measures body shape in still pictures of several worms. Second, it studies swimming behavior in liquid in fine detail. Third, it follows crawling worms and measures their body posture in low-resolution pictures that show a wide area. Fourth, during calcium imaging, it traces the separate parts of the nerve precisely and measures how the head moves.

To see how well TWARDIS performs, we compare it with the older brightness-based method. Published deep learning tools claim that they need retraining for each set of conditions before they can do these tasks. So, for methods that do not need retraining on a new collection of pictures before they can trace the worm, the brightness-based method is the most practical point of comparison. The quality of the pictures still sets the basic limits of what can be achieved. Even so, our approach works in many more situations and needs less setup across a wide range of experimental conditions. In every use we show, TWARDIS also reduces the need for people to step in by hand. This helps solve a basic problem: C. elegans experiments produce huge numbers of pictures, but analyzing them takes a lot of work. Because the system is written entirely in Python and can run on more powerful computers, many different users can use it. As foundation models keep improving, TWARDIS will gain these advances automatically, without needing to be rebuilt from the ground up, so it can keep up with changing needs. This work shows that using general-purpose AI through a team of tools, rather than building more and more specialized solutions, can remove some long-standing technical bottlenecks, help more researchers in the community use the tools, and speed up the discovery of new biological knowledge.
parts.methods:
## Materials and methods

### Taking and analyzing still pictures

#### Measuring body shape in still pictures: first set-up

We grew ordinary, wild-type N2 C. elegans worms at 20°C and fed them OP50 E. coli bacteria, as described in Guisnet et al. [45]. To start a batch of worms of the same age, we placed adult worms that were ready to lay eggs on plates for 2 hours. We then moved these worms to fresh plates whenever they needed food during the experiment.

Every 24 hours after that, we placed the worms on pads of 2% agarose, a soft jelly, in a 5 µL drop of 1M sodium azide. Sodium azide is a chemical that stops the worms from moving. After 1 minute, we carefully soaked up the sodium azide with a Kimwipe, a soft laboratory paper towel. We did not put a coverslip over the worms, because the coverslip squashed them and changed their shape, especially how wide they looked.

From day 3 onward, we focused on the head and the tail, because the worms were too thick to be in focus from end to end. We took pictures within 10 minutes of stopping the worms. We used a grayscale (black-and-white) camera, an Olympus XM10 CCD camera, mounted on an Olympus MVX10 microscope with an MV PLAPO 2XC lens. The pictures were saved as TIF files at 1376 x 1038 pixels, with a 10 ms exposure, using the cellSens software (Evident).

#### Measuring body shape in still pictures: second set-up

We grew C. elegans (N2 wild-type strain) at 20°C on plates of nematode growth medium (NGM), a standard jelly for growing worms, with Escherichia coli OP50 bacteria on it. We obtained worms of the same age as described before [46]. We put the worms to sleep in 0.2% (w/v) levamisole, a drug that stops worms from moving, made up in M9 buffer, a salt solution. We then placed each worm directly between a glass slide and a coverslip.

We took pictures at room temperature with a Leica DMI6000B inverted microscope, which looks up at the sample from below. It had a 4 × /0.10 NA lens, a spinning-disk confocal head (Yokogawa CSU10) and an EM-CCD camera (Hamamatsu ImagEM). Because the worms were too long to fit in one picture, we took several overlapping pictures and joined them into one using Metamorph software, then stitched the tiles together in ImageJ.

#### Testing the brightness-based sorting method.

For both set-ups, we tested the brightness-based sorting method (thresholding) using two options in the Fiji software [33]: the Default option and the Otsu option. Otsu is a standard way of choosing the brightness cut-off automatically.

#### Automatically measuring body shape in pictures of many worms

After taking the pictures of the growing worms, we used the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [19] to automatically make a mask for each picture in our collection. A mask is a map that marks which pixels belong to an object. We used the ViT-H version of SAM with these custom settings: points_per_side: 32, pred_iou_thresh: 0.95, stability_score_thresh: 0.95, min_mask_region_area: 1500. We chose these settings by trial and error, to get the best masks for worm-like objects. We ran SAM with PyTorch [47] and Python 3.10.12 on a graphics card (GPU) that supports CUDA, which makes the processing faster. For each mask SAM made, we cut out the matching part of the original picture. We left out masks that touched the edge of the picture, so that we would not keep pieces of worms.

We had 487 cutouts from the first set-up of the growing worms sorted by hand by C. elegans experts. Each cutout was labeled either “worm” or “not worm” using the LabelBox web tool with academic access [48]. We then split the sorted cutouts at random into two groups: 80% for training and 20% for checking.

To build our worm detector, we used transfer learning. This means we started from a model that had already learned to recognize many kinds of everyday objects, and then retrained it on our own pictures. Our starting model was a Vision Transformer (ViT-H-14) [49] that had been trained beforehand on ImageNet [50], a large collection of everyday photos. We fine-tuned this model on our worm/not-worm pictures. We counted partial worms as “worm” so that the model would be more useful in the future, although we later removed these.

We froze the settings of the starting model, so they could not change, and retrained only the final layer that makes the decision. We also made extra training pictures from the training set by randomly cropping and resizing them and by flipping them left to right. We trained the model for 25 epochs, meaning 25 full passes through the training pictures. To adjust the model, we used stochastic gradient descent (SGD), a standard method that nudges the model step by step to reduce its mistakes. The learning rate, which controls how big each nudge is, was 0.001, and the momentum, which helps the model keep moving in a steady direction, was 0.9. We also used a step learning rate scheduler: every 7 epochs, the learning rate dropped by a factor of 0.1. As the score to be reduced, we used cross-entropy loss, a standard measure of how wrong the model's answers are. We trained on a single GPU using PyTorch. The model that scored best on the checking group, with 100% accuracy, became our final model.

Our worm detector then sorted the masks that SAM had already made into “worm” or “not worm”. Sometimes SAM made several masks for the same worm, each covering a different part of its body. To deal with this, we built an adjacency matrix, a table that records which masks overlap, and then grouped the overlapping masks together. Within each group, we kept only the mask with the largest area, so that each worm was counted only once. SAM already handled worms that were touching each other.

For each worm mask we kept, we measured the following body shape features. The area is the number of pixels inside the mask. The perimeter is the number of pixels along the edge of the shape, measured in a straight-line (Euclidean) way. The medial axis is the longest path along the worm's centerline, which we found by treating the mask as a network of points and links. We sampled 100 points along it. The length is the number of pixels along the medial axis, measured in a straight-line way. The width is estimated at each point along the medial axis.

In pictures that held worms of different ages, we also identified worms by age. For each day of imaging, we used a size limit based on how far a worm's size differed from the sizes of all the worms of the same age that we had identified.

#### Testing how well the system copes with image noise

We took the original 16-bit grayscale pictures and added random speckle (noise) at six increasing levels. The noise came from a Gaussian distribution, a bell-shaped spread of values centered on zero. Its standard deviation (σ), which measures how spread out the noise is, was 655, 1,966, 3,276, 4,587, 6,553 and 13,107 pixel brightness units. These are about 1%, 3%, 5%, 7%, 10% and 20% of the full 16-bit range. We processed each set of noisy pictures with exactly the same settings as for the original pictures.

We judged how well the system did at each noise level by comparing it with the masks made by hand by the experts. We used two measures. The first was the Pearson correlation coefficient, which shows how closely two sets of measurements rise and fall together, where 1 is a perfect match. The second was the percent area agreement for each worm: the area found by the system divided by the area found by hand, multiplied by 100.

To tell apart failures at different stages of the process, we counted two kinds of mistakes separately. A false negative is a real worm that the system misses. A false positive is something the system wrongly calls a worm. We counted false negatives and false positives for the tracing step (whether SAM could make a valid mask for the worm that did not touch the edge of the picture) and for the sorting step (whether our ViT model correctly labeled the worm mask).

#### Measuring how fast the system runs

We took 21 microscope pictures from our collection and processed each one at four sizes: 100%, 90%, 70% and 50% of the original pixel dimensions, which are 1376x1038, 1238x934, 963x726 and 688x519 pixels. We made these smaller pictures by shrinking the image while keeping the overall area the same.

We timed three main steps of the process: SAM2 automatically making masks, the ViT model deciding whether each possible mask is a worm, and (3) measuring the body shape of each worm found. We split the last step into six smaller steps: finding connected pieces, finding the edge and measuring the perimeter, finding the medial axis, cleaning up the ends and branch points of the axis, and measuring width and length along the cleaned-up axis (the worm's centerline).

We ran the GPU tests on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24 GB of graphics memory) using CUDA, with bfloat16 autocast and TF32 precision, which are settings that let the graphics card do the calculations faster. Before timing, we ran a warm-up pass. We ran the CPU tests on the same computer with 4, 8 and 16 threads, which are separate units that can work at the same time. We controlled how many threads ran using PyTorch's threads option (torch.set_num_threads), OpenCV's threads (cv2.setNumThreads) and environment variables (MKL_NUM_THREADS). We also ran the skeleton cleaning step in parallel using a thread pool (concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor). All timing measurements used time.perf_counter(). We did the sorting step in memory, so that reading and writing to the disk would not affect the timing.

### Recording and analyzing swimming in a droplet

#### Setting up the swimming recordings

We grew wild-type N2 C. elegans at 20°C and fed them OP50 E. coli bacteria, as described in Guisnet et al. [45]. We used a large plexiglass dish 10 cm across, which we first cleaned with ethanol and a Kimwipe. We then grounded the dish by bringing its surface very close to a metal cabinet. This removed static electricity from the plexiglass, which helped small droplets stick to the surface. We pipetted 50 µL of filtered NGM liquid onto the center of the dish. We picked young adult worms from their plates and let them wander off their food on an empty agar plate for 2 minutes. Then we moved them into the droplet with a platinum worm pick.

We recorded uncompressed AVI videos for 30 seconds at 10 frames per second, at 2448 x 2048 pixels, with a FLIR Blackfly (BFS-U3-51S5M-C) 5.0 MP camera and Spinnaker SDK software (Teledyne). We held the dish upside down in a custom-made holder and filmed it from below. We placed a ring of LED lights the same size as the dish, centered on it but further up (about 8 centimeters), to reduce light bending (refraction) in the droplet and the plastic dish.

#### Automatically measuring swimming behavior

We traced the worm using Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) [20]. We started the model from a version that had already been trained (sam2_hiera_large.pt) and used CUDA on a graphics card that supports TensorFloat-32. SAM2 needs a prompt, a hint about where the object is. We added a general-purpose prompt frame to every video, which guided the model to the worm automatically. We then carried the tracing backward from the prompt frame through the rest of the video.

To make the tracing more accurate, we did a second round on cropped parts of the video. We applied SAM2 again to these cropped frames, using a new general-purpose prompt frame that matched the crop size, and again carried the tracing backward through the cropped frames. We used the detailed worm masks that resulted for the rest of the analysis.

We cleaned the SAM2 masks from this detailed tracing with morphological operations, simple image-processing steps that remove occasional small specks. We found the worm's skeleton by skeletonizing the mask, which shrinks it down to a one-pixel-wide centerline. We wrote our own method to fix skeletons that touched themselves, so that each frame had a single, continuous skeleton. We smoothed the skeleton points into 100 points using spline interpolation, which fits a smooth curve through the points.

Besides the body shape features described in the section on still pictures, we measured several other things from the skeletons. We calculated Gaussian-weighted curvature along the smoothed skeleton, which shows how sharply the worm bends, using a window of 50 points and a sigma of 10. We measured amplitude along the worm's body as the distance from each skeleton point to the worm's centerline, which we defined as the straight line from head to tail.

We sorted worms by shape using their curvature and amplitude values (Table 4). We chose the cut-offs for this sorting by trial and error. We counted a worm as turned on the z-plane (the flat plane of the picture) if its length was more than 1 standard deviation shorter than the average length in the video. For S-shaped worms, we based the wavelength on the peaks in the curvature; for C-shaped worms we set it at 2 worm lengths, and for straight or turned worms we set it to none. We calculated the wave number as the worm's length divided by the wavelength.

We also studied how the curvature changed over space and over time. For space, we used a Fast Fourier Transform on the curvature data, a method that breaks a pattern into its repeating waves of different sizes. For time, we calculated temporal frequencies from the curvature data. We calculated the power spectral density (PSD) of the normalized curvature over time, which shows how much of the movement comes from each frequency. We used Welch's method with a window size of 30 and an overlap of 25. We then moved a window along the data to find the main frequency in each stretch of time. We found the peaks in the PSD and chose the frequency of the peak with the most power as the main frequency. If there were no peaks, we used the frequency with the most power. Finally, we filled in the main frequencies across the whole video so that every frame had a value.

Table 4

Sorting worms by body shape.

| | 6 | S | U | C | O

| Amplitude | Small | Very small | High | Moderate | High

| Curvature | Very high | Very small | Moderate | Moderate | High

### Recording and analyzing crawling

#### Setting up the crawling recordings

We grew wild-type N2 C. elegans under standard conditions at 20°C and fed them OP50 E. coli bacteria, as described in Guisnet et al. [45]. We picked young adult worms from their plates and let them wander off their food on an empty agar plate for 2 minutes before recording. We recorded AVI videos for 1 minute with the same setup and settings as for swimming.

#### Analyzing the videos with Tierpsy

We installed the version of Tierpsy available on April 23rd 2026 using Docker, a way of running software in a contained package, and used it through its on-screen window, following the instructions on the GitHub page (https://github.com/Tierpsy/tierpsy-tracker) [51]. We chose the brightness-based settings by hand, going through 5 randomly chosen videos, to find the settings that best detected real worms while keeping false alarms from background speckle as low as possible. We then used these settings to analyze all 114 recordings in one batch. We kept all of Tierpsy's default settings except the use_nn_filter option, which we set to False, because keeping it as the default meant that no worms were detected at all.

To measure how well Tierpsy did, we used the timeseries_data from the featuresN output file. We counted a frame as a failure if all of its features were NaN (not a number), however many features were given and which ones.

#### Automatically tracking single worms in fine detail

We tracked the worms in a similar way to swimming, with a few differences for following the path and for handling more complicated body positions. For the detailed tracing, we added two general-purpose prompt frames with complicated shapes to the cropped frames. We then restarted the SAM2 model and applied it to each cropped frame one by one. We carried the tracing through these short cropped sequences to make the detailed masks. We then resized the cropped masks and mapped them back onto the full-size frames for the rest of the analysis.

We measured the body shape features from the skeleton as described in the swimming section, and also measured head bends. In the large pictures, the worm took up so little space that we could not tell the head from the tail by the usual method of comparing brightness [37]. Instead, we used a method that follows the worm over time, looking at movement patterns in a window of 5 frames that slides along the video. We matched the two end points of the skeleton using the Hungarian algorithm, a standard method for pairing things up in the best way. We called the group that moved more the head, based on how far it moved in total. We corrected sudden jumps by checking the recent history and the worm's movement. Then we measured how much the head bent by calculating the angle between the head end point and the main body axis.

To study the path, we used the masks from the shape analysis to find the center of the worm in every frame, by calculating its center of mass. The worm's shape changes, which can make the center of mass jump around. To reduce this noise, we smoothed the paths of the center of mass with a Savitzky-Golay filter, which keeps the real movement patterns while removing fast, jittery noise.

We sorted the worm's movement into three states: moving forward, moving backward and staying still. For each frame, we calculated the worm's speed and direction from the change in the center of mass between that frame and the next. We worked out the direction of movement from the vector from the body's center of mass to the head. When the center of mass moved toward the head, we counted it as moving forward; when it moved away from the head, we counted it as moving backward. When the speed was low (less than 0.6 pixels per frame), we counted it as staying still.

To make sure we sorted the movement correctly, we made some corrections. These were needed during still periods and turns, when the head was harder to detect. We found frames whose movement did not fit the frames around them and corrected them. We grouped unbroken stretches of each kind of movement into bouts. For each bout, we calculated how long it lasted (in frames) and how far the worm went (the total distance traveled). For each video we analyzed, we calculated movement measures such as the total path length, the farthest distance from the starting point, the share of time spent in each state, and the average length of bouts of forward and backward movement.

### Calcium imaging in worms that were partly held in place

#### Watching nerve activity in a small chip

To record calcium activity in the RIA nerve, we used the strain MMH99 (pglr-3a::GCaMP3.3). This strain makes the RIA nerve glow with a calcium-sensitive dye called GCaMP3.3, so that calcium activity shows up as light. We grew the worms under standard conditions at 20°C, fed them OP50 E. coli bacteria and tested them when they were young adults [52].

We filmed the RIA nerve in living worms that were partly held in place, using a microfluidic device, a small chip with tiny channels that carry liquid, as described in Hendricks et al. [53]. We used the MMH99 strain, which makes GCaMP3.3 only in the RIA nerve, to measure calcium activity in the three separate parts of the RIA nerve. Streams of liquid switched back and forth between neutral NGM liquid and IAA (isoamyl alcohol), an odor that attracts worms. The streams flowed past the worm's freely moving head to trigger calcium activity in response to smell [54].

We recorded stacks of 512 x 512 TIFF pictures for each worm over 1 minute, at 10 frames per second with 100 ms exposures. We used an Olympus IX83 inverted microscope with a 40x U-PlanS Apo (N.A. 1.25) silicone immersion lens, a Hammamatsu Orca Flash 4.0LT SCMOS camera and the cellSens software (Evident). A set of solenoid pinch valves (Automate Scientific) switched the streams automatically every 10 seconds.

#### Tracing the nerve parts and measuring head bends by hand

We measured the brightness of the RIA nerve parts and the position of the worm's head by hand, so that we could compare them, using the Fiji software as described in Ouellette et al. [32].

#### Tracing the nerve parts and measuring head bends automatically

We processed the full-frame videos to cut out a region of interest centered on the RIA nerve. As with the other kinds of imaging, we started the SAM2 video model from the Hiera Large version. For each video, we placed a single point on the RIA region in the last frame, and the model carried this point backward through all the frames. We calculated the center of mass of each RIA mask across all frames and used it to set a fixed crop window of 110 × 110 pixels around the RIA region for the whole video.

We wanted to trace three body parts at the same time inside the cropped RIA region: the nerve ring dorsal (nrD), the nerve ring ventral (nrV) and the loop. To do this, we built a system for managing prompts that gave consistent tracing across videos. We added prompt frames marked by experts to the videos to guide the model. We restarted SAM2 with the videos that had these prompts added and with prompts for each body part.

We checked the quality of the tracing carefully to find errors, such as empty masks, regions that were too big, and body parts that overlapped. When needed, we added more prompt frames to the set of prompts. On rare occasions, we filled in a missing mask in a single frame by estimating it from the frames around it. We removed occasional small specks of noise using connected component analysis. We measured brightness from the masks by reading the pixel values from the matching grayscale pictures.

To correct for background brightness, we sampled 100 background regions that were at least 40 pixels away from any traced object, which we found using a distance transform, a method that measures how far each pixel is from the nearest object. We subtracted the average background brightness from the measurements of the objects to get corrected brightness values. The worms sat on either their left or their right side in the chip. So we looked at where the loop sat compared with nrD, and used this to decide whether a head bend was toward the back (dorsal) or toward the belly (ventral).

To study body position, we traced the whole body in the original full-frame videos. We placed a single point on the worm's body and carried it through all frames using SAM2. The masks that resulted captured the whole body, which we used for the head angle analysis. We skeletonized the whole-body masks to get one-pixel-wide centerlines of the worm. For each frame, we calculated the angle between the head and the body, using the front and back parts of the skeleton. We smoothed the angles over time to remove measurement noise while keeping real changes in behavior. We used a small sliding window of 3 frames to remove noise from small changes in the body outline. Finally, we adjusted whether the head angle was positive or negative to match which way the worm was facing, as found in the previous step.

#### Measuring head angle by hand

We picked 50 frames at random from the calcium imaging pictures described above. For each frame, a human expert measured the head angle by hand, finding the tip of the head and drawing a straight reference line along the middle of the body, using the angle tool in Fiji [33]. We took the same 50 frames from both the Fiji ellipse-fitting output and the TWARDIS output. We corrected the angles for the worm's direction and converted them to one shared scale from 0 to 180°, where 90° means a straight head. For each automatic method, we calculated the absolute difference from the angle measured by hand.

### Computers and code

We did all the image analysis, model training and model running on a local computer with Ubuntu 22.04 and one Nvidia RTX 3090 graphics card. To speed things up, we spread some operations across 48 cores working at the same time. For image analysis, we used the Meta SAM model sam_vit_h_4b8939. For video analysis, we downloaded the Meta SAM2 repository and the model from the July 28th 2024 version (https://github.com/facebookresearch/sam2/). We did all the other data analysis and made all the graphs using Python (v3.12.3), uv to manage the software environment, and these freely available libraries: h5py, matplotlib, numpy, OpenCV, pandas, PyTorch, scikit-image, scikit-learn, scipy, seaborn and tqdm [47,55–66]. All our code is freely available at https://github.com/lillyguisnet/TWARDISv0.1. Our fine-tuned worm detector is available on HuggingFace (https://huggingface.co/lillyguisnet/celegans-classifier-vit-h-14-finetuned).
parts.results:
## Results

### Measuring body shape in still pictures of several worms

We first joined the SAM model to our worm classifier, a smaller AI model that we had trained to recognize worms, so that the two could work together to pull out body-shape features from still pictures of worms. SAM first traces the outline of every object in the whole picture. SAM cannot tell which of those objects is a worm, so we then used our trained classifier to pick out the worm outlines (Fig 1A).

We tested this TWARDIS pipeline on worms of many ages, from young larvae (called L1 larvae) to adults 12 days old (Table 1). It traced the worms in the pictures and our classifier picked out the worm outlines successfully. On the pictures we used to train the classifier, it sorted every outline correctly at every age, in a single pass through the model, with no help from people. This shows that the pipeline copes well with common problems in our pictures, such as changing lighting, blurry focus, random speckle (noise) and differences in how the worms were prepared. Some pictures held worms of mixed ages. To pick out only the worms of the age we wanted, we used a size limit for each imaging day: worms that were too big or too small for that day's age group were left out.

The usual method of sorting pixels by brightness, and even newer methods, are easily thrown off by flaws in the picture. For C. elegans pictures, they often fail when parts of the picture are out of focus, when worms lie on top of each other, when the pharynx (the worm's muscular throat) shows a sharp contrast, or when the picture is noisy. Researchers then have to set up their experiments very carefully to get nearly perfect pictures, and then sort through the results by hand or automatically to throw away bad samples [2–4].

The pictures in Fig 1B–F show these advantages. Raw pictures with worms lying on top of each other and with noise give broken or wrong outlines when sorted by brightness. Our version of TWARDIS, by contrast, gives clean, accurate outlines without any help from people, such as clicking on objects or marking areas of interest [6,24]. We also tested our worm classifier on a second set of pictures taken with a different recording setup. It made no false positives (it never marked something as a worm that was not one) and had fewer than 5% false negatives (it missed less than 5% of the worms that were really there). This shows that the classifier had learned very little about the particular look of the pictures in our training set (Fig 1D–F).

From these outlines, we measured key body-shape features: area, perimeter (the length of the outline), length and width, along the whole length of the worm. This took very little extra computing. When we compared our TWARDIS measurements with measurements made by people tracing by hand, the correlation was 0.999 (Fig 1G, Table 2). No picture in our datasets could be traced correctly by sorting pixels by brightness alone. This shows that our method greatly reduces the need to prepare carefully before recording or to spend time handling the pictures afterwards (Fig 1B–F).

To find out how much image quality our pipeline can tolerate, we added more and more artificial Gaussian noise, from σ = 655 to σ = 13,107 (Fig 1G and 1H, Table 2). At moderate noise levels (σ up to 1,966), the pipeline kept working very well. It had 0% false negatives, fewer than 5% false positives from the classifier, and a tracing correlation above 0.999 with the hand-traced outlines.

As the noise grew stronger (σ = 3,276 to 6,553), false negatives began to appear, both from tracing failures and from labeling failures. For the worms that were still found, the tracing quality stayed high (R ≥ 0.988). At the strongest noise level (σ = 13,107), only 33% of the worms were found, but for those worms the correlation with the hand-traced outlines stayed high (R ≥ 0.998), and there were no false positives.

For measuring features in numbers, it is better to miss some worms than to measure them wrongly. Missing worms keeps the data honest, at the cost of processing fewer worms, rather than adding errors.

Because this approach is fully automatic, it removes the need for people to step in. It also reduces the differences and bias that come from different people tracing the same worm [25,26]. For example, if several researchers trace the outline of the same worm, by hand or by sorting pixels by brightness, they will always place the edges slightly differently, and this can make the measured features vary (Fig 1I). The average percent area agreement between TWARDIS and the hand-traced outlines (Table 2) also shows this: the quality of the picture affects how clear the edges are. Our method, in contrast, uses the same approach for every user and every dataset, which reduces bias.

Most importantly, our automation makes processing time unimportant. The pipeline is fully automatic, can run many pictures at the same time, and works on both ordinary computer processors (CPUs) and graphics cards (GPUs). The SAM models need about 0.5 GB of memory and our trained classifier about 2.5 GB. This means TWARDIS can process any amount of data, at a speed that grows with the computer available (S1 Fig).

### Measuring swimming behavior in numbers

We then used our approach on videos of C. elegans swimming in upside-down droplets of liquid (Fig 2A). This kind of recording brings new challenges. The worms sometimes touch themselves into extreme O-shapes or 6-shapes, their outlines are faint, the light bending through the droplet creates changing noise, the background flickers, and stray particles move around. Current ways of analyzing swimming rely on sorting pixels by brightness and on comparing pixels between frames to follow the worm. These methods cope less well with imperfect conditions, so researchers have to throw away frames or step in by hand to keep the results accurate [7,27].

Our TWARDIS version, by contrast, handled these challenges without throwing away any frames or any manual tuning. It produced sharp outlines that captured the worm's shape accurately, even in a low-resolution picture where the worm took up only a very small part of the whole view (about 0.25%) (Fig 2F and S1 Movie). Our approach gave more complete outlines of the body (Fig 2G–K).

Fig 2

It contains outlines of the objects of interest, which the model uses to find and trace the same objects in frames that have no outlines. Then SAM2 (the video version of SAM) follows the worm through the recording. A crop of the video is made around the tracked worm. A reference picture of the same size is added to the crop and passed through SAM2 to trace the worm in fine detail. Finally, features are measured for each frame. A small red picture-in-picture of the worm is shown for reference. (B–E) Selected features over time from a one-minute recording at 10 frames per second of a wild-type worm swimming in a liquid droplet. (B) Shape label for each frame, based on amplitude and curvature. (C) Largest bend in each frame: the greatest distance, measured at right angles, between points along the worm's body and a straight line from head to tail. From these sharp outlines, we drew worm skeletons, as described above. A skeleton is a line running along the middle of the body. It let us calculate a wide range of other behavior features accurately, such as curvature along the body, amplitude (the distance from the body's centerline) and wavelength. Because the outlines were so good, the skeletons were more accurate too. We no longer had to throw away frames because the shape was poorly captured, and we could measure features continuously over time and time behaviors precisely (Fig 2B–E).

For example, deep 6-shaped bends show up as periods of very high curvature and small amplitude, while O-shaped bends have both high curvature and high amplitude (Fig 2G and 2K, S1 Movie). Using a single inexpensive camera, ordinary LED lighting and a simple setup, we measured features in detail without costly or careful preparation, and without any manual sorting of the results.

### Tracking a single worm crawling in fine detail

Next, we extended our process to videos of C. elegans crawling on agar plates, in open spaces. As in our swimming recordings, the worms took up only a small part of the whole view (Fig 3A and 3B). These simple recording conditions also cost little in equipment and took little time to prepare. Again, the usual method of sorting pixels by brightness typically struggles here. It produces noisy or incomplete outlines when the worm touches itself or when there are flaws in the background, which often leads to throwing away frames, relying on manual corrections or using expensive recording equipment [28–30].

For example, we took 114 one-minute recordings of wild-type worms in our conditions. A popular brightness-based worm tracker called Tierpsy gave features across the whole recording for only 76.3% of these recordings, and how complete those features were varied a lot. On average, the tracker failed to find the worm for 2.01% of each recording (SD ± 9.78%), ranging from 0% to 96.33% (n = 114 one-minute recordings at 10 frames per second). Our automatic approach, however, solved these problems without any manual corrections or thrown-away frames, and produced clean outlines even in our imperfect conditions (Fig 3B).

Fig 3

Tracking a single worm.

(A) How the analysis works. First, a set of reference pictures (a “generic prompt frame pool”) is added to the video. These are chosen to cover the range of positions the object of interest can take, giving the model many examples to learn from and making it more accurate. Then SAM2 follows the worm through the recording. A crop of the video is made around the tracked worm. A reference picture pool of the same size is added to the crop and passed through SAM2 to trace the worm in fine detail. The detailed outline is then placed back onto the original video. Finally, body features and path features are measured for each frame. A small red picture-in-picture of the worm is shown for reference. (B) Example frame showing how little of the picture the worm takes up, with outlines traced by TWARDIS and by sorting pixels by brightness. (C) The worm's path, colored by the type of movement from (F), with each point one frame. Start and end points are labeled. The X and Y axes show position in pixels. Positive and negative values mean bends to either side, but the belly side and back side are not told apart. Points along the trace mark the peaks and dips used to measure head bending. From these high-quality outlines, we could measure the same body features as in swimming, plus a set of path features across frames, such as head bending angles, speed and the full path of the worm (Fig 3C–F). This let us study body shape reliably while also following the path, with every frame included. It removed the common trade-off between tracking only the center point of the worm, which is more common with cheap, basic systems, and capturing full body posture, which usually needs more expensive equipment [31]. By giving sharp outlines and a wide range of features from simple equipment, with no manual corrections, our TWARDIS approach bridges the gap between easy access, precision and the time spent on manual analysis (S2 Movie).

### Tracing the body in calcium imaging of worms partly held in place

Finally, we used our approach to pull out glowing-dye signals and head movements from calcium imaging of C. elegans that were partly held in place in microfluidic devices, which are tiny channels that carry liquids. In particular, we tracked the glow of three parts of the RIA nerve cell (called nrV, nrD and the loop) in a device that switched between streams of different smells while the worm's head was free to move (Fig 4A and 4B) [32]. Our automatic approach traced each part of the nerve frame by frame, giving precise outlines even though the shape of the nerve cell changed during the recording. We gave the model a set of about 20 pictures, labeled by an expert, to show it where the edges of each part lay. This gave us detailed, precise brightness measurements of the calcium signal (Fig 4C and S3 Movie).

The usual tools for this kind of analysis are ImageJ (Fiji), Matlab or OpenCV software. Their add-ons or functions use image registration, which lines up the same body parts across frames, so that the brightness can be measured inside a chosen small patch of the image, called a region of interest (ROI) [33]. However, these methods usually struggle to line up body parts whose shape changes from frame to frame, such as the three parts of the RIA nerve cell. People can correct this by hand, but it takes much more time.

If these problems are not noticed, errors creep into the data. In most cases, the nerve part briefly moves outside the chosen patch, which causes a sudden, artificial drop in the measured brightness, and the whole signal trace ends up flattened (Fig 4D). The loop part is especially dim at rest, so it is especially easily harmed by a poorly chosen patch. When we compared the loop brightness traces from TWARDIS with those from Fiji, the TWARDIS traces differed from the average by a similar or larger amount (the mean absolute difference), which shows that our approach flattened the signal less artificially (Fig 4E).

Fig 4

SAM2 follows the worm through the recording, and the worm outlines are used to measure head angles. Separately, a reference picture of the RIA region is added to the video, and SAM2 follows the RIA region through the original recording. A crop of the video is made around the tracked RIA region. A reference picture pool of the same size, showing the three parts of the RIA nerve cell, is added to the crop and passed through SAM2 to trace the parts in fine detail. The detailed outlines are used to measure brightness activity in the original recording. (B) Example frame from a calcium imaging recording, with brightness boosted so it is easier to see. The close-up shows the three traced parts of the RIA nerve cell, whose brightness over time is shown in (C). (C) Head bending and brightness over time from a one-minute recording at 10 frames per second of a wild-type worm in a microfluidic device, with the RIA nerve cell carrying the glowing dye GCaMP3.3. Blue traces are data from Fiji and orange traces are data from TWARDIS. Shaded areas show when the positive smell was present. Top panel: head position from Fiji (on a scale from -1 to 1) and from TWARDIS (in degrees relative to the body). Second, third and fourth panels: brightness of nrD, nrV and the loop, respectively, each scaled to its own range. (D) Example brightness trace of the loop part, where the Fiji data is artificially flattened because the nerve part briefly moved outside the chosen patch. (E) Average absolute difference from the mean for the loop part, comparing Fiji with TWARDIS. n = 22 recordings. (F–G) Example traces where the head positions from Fiji and TWARDIS are clearly different. (H) Example head positions from (G), with values from Fiji and TWARDIS. (I) Scatterplot of head angles from Fiji compared with TWARDIS. Fiji values (on a scale from -1 to 1) are converted to a scale from 0 to 180 for comparison. 90 means a perfectly straight head, and 0 and 180 degrees mean the most extreme bending. r = 0.884. n = 13,486 frames from 22 recordings.

Tracing the whole body in our approach let us follow head movement accurately by drawing the skeleton and calculating angles, which gives measurements that are more meaningful for biology. Earlier standard approaches estimate head position by fitting an ellipse (an oval) to the worm's head after sorting the pixels by brightness, and then using the line through the middle of that ellipse. These values are then rescaled to the smallest and largest values in each recording, to estimate head position on a scale of 180 degrees. TWARDIS, on the other hand, gives the head's actual angle relative to the middle line of the body. This gives much more accurate and useful information for testing ideas than rescaling within each recording (Fig 4C, 4F and 4G).

In general, the Fiji ellipse method estimates deeper head bends than our TWARDIS approach. The correlation between the two approaches was 0.884 overall, and only 0.746 when the direction of the head bend was ignored (Figs 4I and S2). These differences stand out most in recordings where the worm's head bends only a little, or only on one side, because there the head angles from the two methods drift apart most (Fig 4F–H and S3 Movie).

To compare the two approaches further, we calculated the percent agreement between the Fiji and TWARDIS signals for each nerve part and for head angle (average percent agreement ± SD: nrD: 96.43 ± 3.38; nrV: 96.02 ± 3.54; loop: 86.11 ± 16.40; head angle: 85.62 ± 9.66). The gaps between the two methods show the limits of the approach based on a chosen small patch of the image. In particular, the low agreement and large spread for the loop brightness and the head angle fit the flattened signals and inflated head angles that we described above.

In the same way, we compared both methods with head angles measured by people in 50 randomly chosen frames (S3 Fig). TWARDIS head angles agreed much more closely with the human measurements than the Fiji head angles did. The average absolute difference from the human measurements was 6.20° ± 5.56° for TWARDIS and 22.98° ± 16.42° for Fiji. However, measuring head angles by hand is itself affected by the observer's bias and by how clearly the line can be placed, as we discussed for tracing body outlines (Fig 1I). So human measurements should not be treated as the absolute correct answer.

## Discussion Measuring the body shape, behavior and nerve activity of C. elegans in numbers is what makes this worm so useful for research. Yet the tools researchers use to do this have often faced a trade-off between three things: how precise they are, how many pictures they can handle quickly, and how easy they are to use. Traditional methods often need very carefully controlled experiments, expensive equipment, or a lot of work by hand [2,5,30]. Existing tools can also be hard to set up, keep running or change. Some depend on software that others sell and control, some need to be retrained for each new experimental setup, and some need complicated programming environments such as MATLAB, Java, C++ or Docker [27,28,34–37]. In this study we introduce the first version of TWARDIS (Tools for Worm Automated Recognition & Dynamic Imaging System). It is a set of analysis tools written in Python, built from separate parts that can be swapped or upgraded. It uses large AI image models to measure the worm's features automatically and with high precision, across many different kinds of imaging. In this way it tackles some of the main bottlenecks: the time researchers spend on repetitive, hand-made image analysis, and the equipment they need. We show that TWARDIS traces the worm's body reliably and accurately in four different kinds of imaging: measuring body shape in still pictures, swimming behavior, crawling behavior, and calcium imaging. It does this with little or no help from people (Table 3). **Table 3. Almost all current tools for this step rely on sorting pixels by brightness, or on simple methods that look for basic features. This is true even of newer tools that use neural networks to follow worms [3,13,17,28]. Several recent tools do use deep learning (a powerful kind of AI) for later tasks, such as sorting shapes into types or keeping track of which worm is which. But these tools work on outlines that were already traced by sorting pixels by brightness. So the weakness of the first step remains, and these tools are just as fragile: they are easily thrown off by changes in lighting, by poor focus, by bits of debris, and by random speckle in the image [3,11–18]. When these brightness-based methods fail, researchers have to correct the results by hand, throw away frames, or spend a lot of time adjusting settings. This slows the work down and can bring in bias. On the other hand, tools that use deep learning to replace the tracing step report that they need to be retrained for each new experimental setup. This makes them impractical for many researchers, because of technical limits or because they need very large collections of example pictures [6,8,10]. TWARDIS uses the Segment Anything Models (SAMs) [19,20], and in this way it gets past many of the problems described above. It copes remarkably well with several common imaging problems. In our tests on still pictures of body shape, TWARDIS sorted out worms lying on top of each other and noisy backgrounds, at every life stage, in cases where sorting pixels by brightness failed (Fig 1B–F). For still pictures, we combined SAM with a smaller AI model that we trained to recognize worms automatically. This team of tools worked well across our different recording setups. Automating the work speeds up analysis, but it also makes results much easier to repeat, because it removes the differences between people that come from tracing worms by hand or adjusting brightness settings (Fig 1I) [25,26]. A big advantage of TWARDIS, as a team of AI tools, is that it can pull out detailed behavior data from simple, low-cost recording setups. Detailed study of body posture has often been limited to expensive systems with high magnification. Cheap recordings that show a wide area, but in low detail, usually allow only tracking the center point of the worm [5]. TWARDIS bridges this gap. It successfully analyzed both swimming and crawling even when the worm took up only about 0.25% of the whole picture (Figs 2F and 3B). Because SAM traced the worm so well, it could pick out complicated body postures (Fig 2G–2K). This precision lets us tell apart subtle kinds of behavior. For example, it can tell a deep 6-shaped bend (strongly curved, but small in size) from an O-shape (strongly curved, and large) (Fig 2G and 2K). Importantly, TWARDIS picked out the same features as other tools, but it did not throw away any frames or need corrections by hand. This keeps the video unbroken in time, which is essential for studying sequences of behavior and how they change, such as the tortuosity analysis we presented in [38]. Tortuosity measures how twisty a path is, and it was only possible with complete tracks (Figs 2B–E and 3C–F). Using TWARDIS on calcium imaging in living worms shows even more clearly how precise it is in difficult, changing situations. In worms that are partly held in place, the parts of a nerve change shape and move during recording. One example is the RIA interneuron, a nerve cell with three long branches called axons. Pulling out the glow from these parts is hard, because the parts bend and shift while the recording is going. The usual approach is to measure only a fixed small patch of the image, as in the program Fiji. This often fails to keep up with the changes, so the patch ends up out of line with the nerve. The result is that the glow seems weaker than it really is when the part briefly leaves the patch, or the researcher has to spend a lot of time correcting the results (Fig 4D). TWARDIS, guided by carefully chosen starting points (prompt engineering), traces the nerve parts frame by frame and adjusts as they move, capturing their shape accurately. This gave a more faithful picture of how calcium levels changed over time. We can see this in the reduced false flattening of the signal, which often happens in the RIA loop, the part of the RIA nerve cell that runs in a loop (Fig 4E). TWARDIS also greatly improves how we measure behavior during calcium imaging. We showed that the standard method, which fits an oval (an ellipse) to the head after sorting pixels by brightness, often makes head bends look bigger than they are (Fig 4F–I). TWARDIS, in contrast, uses an accurate trace of the whole body to work out the head's absolute angle compared with the middle line of the body. This gives a measure that is easier to understand and more meaningful for the biology (Fig 4H). Such a measure is essential for linking nerve activity precisely with the behavior the worm produces. Our step-by-step test of how noise affects the results makes clear the practical limits of our approach. The system kept its measurements accurate at noise levels well beyond those seen in everyday imaging. When it did fail, it mostly played it safe: as image quality got worse, it missed worms rather than tracing them wrongly. This test also shows clearly that TWARDIS is not immune to poor images: pictures of very low quality will give incomplete data. So our tool makes the need for reasonable imaging conditions less strict, but it does not remove it. The success of TWARDIS shows the advantage of building a team of AI tools on top of a powerful, general-purpose foundation model. The Segment Anything Models were already trained on a huge collection of very high-quality pictures. Because of this, they trace outlines extremely well in many situations, without the long, setup-specific training that many other deep learning tools need [3,6,8,11,12,17]. We make use of this general power and add targeted strategies (a simple worm-recognition model and prompt engineering) and fixed, step-by-step workflows to reach high performance. This design makes the system easy to move to different imaging setups. It is also built from separate parts, so both the pre-trained models and the fixed workflows can be changed or improved. As newer versions of SAM and similar models work better while needing less computing power, TWARDIS will gain these improvements without any major rebuilding. The worm-recognition model needs at least 4GB of computer memory (RAM). The TWARDIS workflow can run on both ordinary processors (CPUs) and graphics cards (GPUs), and its work can be split up to run at the same time. So, like other tools that can scale up and run on GPUs, it can benefit from powerful hardware. That said, because the system no longer needs a person to step in, processing time hardly matters: analyses can run without any input from the user, for example overnight. TWARDIS brings big improvements, but we see room for future development. Today, the early v0.1 TWARDIS scripts are available in a public online store (https://github.com/lillyguisnet/TWARDISv0.1). In the future, we plan to release TWARDIS as an easy-to-use, open-source Python package, so that many more people can use it and it becomes easier to reach. We hope this package could also serve as building blocks for future teams of AI tools. To make the tools even easier to start with, a web-based window with buttons and menus could be built, using the user's own computer. It could even use the computer's graphics card through the web, with technologies such as WebGPU. This could make the tools available to researchers who have never used command lines. Our results showed a small amount of overfitting to the particular look of the pictures in our training collection, and tracing failures in damaged images (Fig 1 and Table 2). Overfitting happens when a model learns the quirks of its training pictures too closely and then does worse on new ones. These problems can easily be fixed by training our worm-recognition model and the SAMs further on worm pictures from public collections, with artificial damage added to make the collection more varied. Another option, to remove completely any bias tied to one particular setup, would be to replace the worm-recognition step with a small but general vision-language model, a model that can understand both pictures and words. It could be reached through online services or run on the user's own computer. Also, our way of identifying worms by age is tuned for worm strains that develop evenly. Worms with very uneven growth patterns might not be sorted correctly. Right now, the system is tuned for finding several worms in still pictures, and for recording one worm swimming, one worm crawling, and the glow of the RIA nerve cell. Future versions could add tracking several worms at once, swimming in plates with many small wells, many different ways of recording nerve activity, adjustments for worms with very abnormal body shapes, or even calcium activity in worms that move freely, as we presented in [39]. Extending the moving-worm analyses to several worms at the same time brings challenges of a different kind. The system has to keep track of which worm is which from frame to frame, untangle worms that stay on top of each other for a long time, work out the shape of a worm hidden behind another, and recognize a worm again once it is no longer hidden. These challenges need specially designed models, not just tracing. Future approaches for several moving worms should build on recent computer vision methods made for similar problems, such as trackers that remember past positions of many objects, specialized methods for estimating body posture, and methods for tracing skeletons and untangling overlapping worms [40–43]. In the same way, amodal completion, which means guessing the full shape of an object that is partly hidden from the parts we can see, could make it possible to count worms or measure their shape in pictures crowded with many worms [44]. However, this approach needs careful checking in a scientific setting, because guessed shapes risk bringing in steady measurement errors, especially for worms with abnormal body shapes. In addition, adapting the system to follow glowing signals in 3D imaging or in freely moving worms would mean combining it with other methods that solve different problems from tracing, such as correcting for movement, separating signals that overlap, and mapping where the nerves are. In conclusion, TWARDIS offers a strong, precise and automatic way to measure the features of C. elegans. By making the most of large AI image models, our team of tools gets past the built-in weaknesses of traditional tracing. This allows detailed analysis even when imaging conditions are not perfect and when low-cost equipment is used. TWARDIS greatly reduces the work done by hand and improves the quality of the data. It opens the way for large studies that can be repeated, so that researchers can focus on designing experiments and understanding the biology, rather than on processing images by hand.
